While they touch, electrons flow from the negative sphere into the positive one until the identical spheres share the total equally:

q=(+6)+(−2)2=+2.0 nC eachq = \frac{(+6) + (-2)}{2} = +2.0\ \text{nC each}q=2(+6)+(−2)​=+2.0 nC each

Each sphere is left short of 1.25 × 1010 electrons: like the positive ion, short one electron, many times over.

probability-3-06.solution:
μX = Σ xP(x) = 0(0.50) + 1(0.30) + 2(0.15) + 3(0.05) = 0.75.

1.50 averages the values as if they were equally likely. 0.25 averages the probabilities. 0.188 divides ΣxP(x) by the number of values, as for a list of data; the probabilities already do the weighting.

collecting-6-01.solution:
Random assignment means a significant difference can be attributed to the amount of sleep: cause and effect. But the subjects were volunteers, not a random sample of adults, so the conclusion reaches only people like these volunteers.

Generalizing to all adults would need random selection. A correlation-only conclusion undersells the random assignment, and saying neither is justified ignores it.

twovar-1-06.solution:
‘Of all the students’ makes this a joint relative frequency: 46/400 = 0.115.

0.307 divides by the 150 11th graders: the proportion of 11th graders who play. 0.287 divides by the 160 players: the proportion of players in 11th grade. 0.375 is the marginal proportion of 11th graders, players or not.

probability-1-05.solution:
There are 36 equally likely ordered outcomes. Sums of 10 or more: (4, 6), (6, 4), (5, 5), (5, 6), (6, 5), (6, 6): six of them. P = 6/36 = 0.167.

3/36 counts each sum once instead of each outcome. 3/11 treats the eleven sums 2–12 as equally likely, which they are not. 4/21 treats unordered pairs as equally likely, but (4, 6) can happen two ways and (5, 5) only one.

sampling-1-01.solution:
This is sampling variability: each random sample includes different individuals, so a statistic such as x̄ differs from sample to sample even when both samples are done correctly.

Nothing suggests an error; two correct random samples rarely agree. The population mean is a fixed parameter for the night in question. Samples of 30 give useful estimates; they just vary, and that variation can be described.

sampling-2-02.solution:
z = (40 − 42)/5 = −0.40 and (50 − 42)/5 = 1.60. The area between them is 0.9452 − 0.3446 = 0.6006.

0.9452 is everything below 50 cm; 0.6554 everything above 40 cm. 0.2898 drops the minus sign of the lower z.

collecting-1-01.solution:
Each SRS is a different random set of students, so p̂ changes from sample to sample: sampling variability. With samples of 20, a difference of 20 percentage points happens by chance quite often.

Bias is a systematic error of a method; two honest SRSs can still differ. Nothing suggests the population changed. A small sample is variable, not useless: its p̂ still estimates p.

twovar-5-02.solution:
r2 is the fraction of the variation in the response (about its mean) that the linear model with the explanatory variable accounts for.

It is not a share of days predicted exactly; on most days the prediction is off by some amount. It is not a share of drinks, and a regression on observational data does not show cause. The correlation is √0.64 = 0.80, not 0.64.

probability-2-06.solution:
Two branches of the tree end in “on time”. Multiply along each and add: 0.8(0.9) + 0.2(0.5) = 0.72 + 0.10 = 0.82.

0.70 averages the two conditional probabilities as if good and bad days were equally common. 0.72 counts only good days. 0.45 multiplies two conditional probabilities that belong to different branches.

collecting-4-04.solution:
Double-blind: both the subjects and those who interact with them or evaluate their responses are kept unaware of who got which treatment, so neither expectations nor judgement can favour one treatment.

Only the subjects not knowing is single-blind. Blinding is about treatments, not the hypothesis. The number of control groups has nothing to do with blinding.

collecting-2-03.solution:
Without replacement the first name is not put back, so the second draw is from 29 names, 11 of them seniors: (12/30)(11/29) = 0.152.

0.160 is with replacement. 0.166 takes one less name but forgets one less senior. 0.400 is the chance for one draw only.

twovar-3-03.solution:
r gives direction (negative) and strength (0.78: moderately strong) of a linear association, in context.

The percent of variation explained is r2 = 0.61, not |r|. These are observational data, so they cannot show cause: a lurking variable, such as time spent on homework, may explain both. A change in GPA per hour is a slope, which needs the standard deviations: b = r sy/sx.

twovar-2-05.solution:
Each extra year lowers the price by about the same amount (1.9 to 2.3 thousand dollars), so the points fall steadily along a line: negative, linear, and strong (r = −1.000).

Prices fall as age rises, so the direction is not positive. The points lie very close to a line, so the association is not weak. The drop per year is roughly constant, not changing, so the form is not curved.

probability-4-06.solution:
X, the number correct, is binomial: 10 independent questions, each correct with probability 0.25. P(X = 3) = C(10, 3)(0.25)3(0.75)7 = 120 × 0.002086 = 0.2503.

0.7759 is P(X ≤ 3), the cumulative probability. 0.0021 is one particular order of rights and wrongs, without counting the 120 orders. 0.0156 ignores the wrong answers.

means-6-01.solution:
t = (x̄1 − x̄2 − 0)/√(s12/n1 + s22/n2) = 3.5/√(1.2013 + 2.0089) = 3.5/1.7917 = 1.953.

1.393 adds the two standard errors instead of the variances. 1.090 forgets the square root. 0.360 uses the standard deviations without dividing by the sample sizes.

sampling-6-02.solution:
Both populations are normal, so x̄A − x̄B is normal with mean 2 mL and SD 1.414 mL. P(x̄A − x̄B < 0): z = (0 − 2)/1.414 = −1.41, area 0.079.

0.159 adds the standard deviations. 0.345 ignores the sample sizes. 0.921 is the probability that A’s mean is the larger.

chisquare-2-05.solution:
A p-value is computed assuming H0 is true. It is the probability, under that assumption, of a statistic as large as the one observed or larger.

It is not the probability that H0 is true or false: H0 was assumed, not tested for probability. Nor is it computed assuming the claim is wrong.

proportions-2-04.solution:
The interval is an estimate of the parameter, the proportion of all adults in the city, stated with the confidence level: “95% confident … captures the true proportion”.

The sample proportion is known exactly (0.580): no probability is needed for it. The interval is not about individual adults. Nor does it say where 95% of sample proportions fall: those are centred on p, not on this sample’s p̂.

means-4-06.solution:
The interval estimates the difference of the two population means, in the stated order. It contains both negative and positive values, so it allows men to sleep less, the same, or more.

“Between −0.22 and 0.84 hours less” ignores that the interval runs past 0 to +0.22. The interval is about means, not individuals. And a confidence interval gives no probability that the difference is any one value.

chisquare-5-02.solution:
0.044 < 0.05, so reject H0: there is convincing evidence of an association in the population.

This is an observational sample, so it shows association, not cause, and a test never proves anything. Since p < α, failing to reject is wrong. Independence is H0, the statement being rejected.

means-4-01.solution:
The same patients are measured twice: paired data. The differences before − after are 6, 4, 3, 9, 3, 11, -1, 8, with x̄d = 5.375 and sd = 3.889. t = 5.375/(3.889/√8) = 3.91, df = 7.

0.96 treats before and after as independent samples, so the large patient-to-patient spread swamps the change. 1.38 forgets the √n. 5.53 counts 16 observations, but there are only 8 differences.

proportions-4-06.solution:
A larger sample narrows both sampling distributions, so more of the 0.3 distribution lies beyond the cut-off: power 0.937, up from 0.735.

A smaller α moves the cut-off out (power 0.494). A two-sided test splits α between the tails, moving the upper cut-off out too. An alternative closer to 0.25 is harder to detect (power 0.241).

proportions-3-06.solution:
A p-value is computed assuming H0 is true: the chance of a result at least as extreme as the one observed, in the direction of Ha.

It is not the probability that H0 is true; H0 is assumed, not assessed. “Happened by chance alone” leaves out both the assumption and the “or more extreme”. It is not a proportion of phones.

sampling-4-02.solution:
The standard deviation of p̂ measures how far sample proportions typically fall from p in repeated random samples of the same size.

It is not itself a proportion of students. “Every sample” is too strong: many samples fall farther than one standard deviation away. It says nothing about change over time; p is fixed.

proportions-5-04.solution:
0 is a plausible value of the difference, so the data do not give convincing evidence of a difference.

How much of the interval lies above 0 does not matter: any value inside is plausible. A plausible 0 is not a proven 0: the interval also allows differences up to 0.12. Width alone does not rule out conclusions.

chisquare-4-01.solution:
Three separate samples, one categorical variable (favourite sport), and the question is whether its distribution is the same in each population: homogeneity.

Independence needs one sample with two variables recorded for each person. Goodness of fit compares one sample with a claimed distribution. A two-sample z test handles two groups and a two-category variable, not three schools and four sports.

means-1-03.solution:
With s in place of σ, the statistic (x̄ − μ)/(s/√n) has a t distribution with 7 degrees of freedom, whose tails are heavier. The right critical value is t* = 2.365; with 1.96 the intervals are too narrow and capture μ only about 91% of the time.

s is not usually larger than σ; in small samples it is more often smaller. A normal population makes the t procedure exact, not the z one. And x̄ is an unbiased estimate of μ at any sample size.

means-2-06.solution:
The confidence level is a property of the method: in repeated sampling, 95% of the intervals it produces capture μ. (A simulation like the chapter’s opening figure shows it.)

The interval is about the mean, not the individual data values. The sample mean is always inside its own interval: it is the centre. And there is only one population mean; it is fixed, not spread over the interval.

slopes-5-06.solution:
Two quantitative variables on each bird, and the question asks for a rate of change: the slope of the population regression line, estimated by b ± t*SEb.

There are not two groups to compare. A mean body mass ignores wingspan. A chi-square test is for categorical variables, and it is a test, not an estimate.

ecology-1-01.solution: The expected count on each side is 20. χ² = (26 − 20)²/20 + (14 − 20)²/20 = 3.60. Because 3.60 < 3.84, the difference could be due to chance, and the null hypothesis is not rejected. Concluding a preference is the error of reading χ² the wrong way round. 1.80 uses only the moist side; every category contributes. 7.20 divides by 10 instead of the expected count 20.

slopes-1-02.solution:
At 4 years the mean price is 21000 − 1500(4) = $15000. Then z = (16000 − 15000)/1200 = 0.83, and P(z > 0.83) = 0.2023.

0.2525 divides by the size of the slope, 1500, as if it were the standard deviation. 0.7977 is the proportion below $16000. 0.0478 divides σ by √4, as if the age were a sample size; σ is the spread of individual prices.

bonding-1-01.solution:
Bond polarity grows with the electronegativity difference. C–O: 0.89; N–H: 0.84; C–Cl: 0.61; O–F: 0.54. C–O has the largest difference.

N–H is close but smaller. C–Cl looks polar because chlorine is very electronegative, but carbon is not far behind. O–F joins the two most electronegative atoms, which nearly cancel: fluorine’s large value does not make every bond to it the most polar.

slopes-3-04.solution:
0 lies inside (−0.171, 1.331), so a slope of 0, no linear relationship, is plausible. The evidence is not convincing.

Plausible is not proven: a value inside the interval is not shown to be true. How much of the interval lies above 0 does not matter; whether 0 is in it does. A positive sample slope can happen by chance when β = 0.

genes-1-01.solution:
In double-stranded DNA every G pairs with a C, so C is also 22%. G + C = 44%, leaving 56% for A + T, which are equal: A = 28%.

22% assumes all four bases are equally common or that A pairs with G. 78% subtracts only the G. 56% is A + T together, not A alone.

biochem-1-01.solution:
The O–H bonds are polar covalent: the electrons are shared, but unequally, because oxygen attracts them more strongly. That gives oxygen a partial negative charge (δ−) and each hydrogen a partial positive charge (δ+).

No electrons are fully transferred, so the bonds are not ionic. Hydrogen bonds are a consequence of the partial charges, not their cause. The molecule as a whole is neutral: it has exactly as many electrons as protons.

heredity-1-01.solution:
Meiosis I separates homologues, so each cell after it has n = 8 chromosomes, but each chromosome still has the two sister chromatids made in S phase. Meiosis II then separates the sisters.

In prophase I and in G2 the cell still has all 16 chromosomes. A gamete after meiosis II has 8 chromosomes of one chromatid each.

signaling-1-01.solution:
Light per cell is 0.0002 units at 105 cells per mL but 0.04 at 109: it jumps 200-fold between 107 and 108. And cell-free medium from a dense culture switches on a sparse one. So something the cells release, not the cells themselves, is the trigger, and it works only above a threshold concentration: quorum sensing.

Light per cell is not constant, as the table shows. The filtered medium had no cells to touch, so contact is not needed (and bacteria have no gap junctions). A count of divisions would not let cell-free medium start the glow.

slopes-3-01.solution:
b ± t*SEb with df = n − 2 = 13: t* = 2.160, so 0.2613 ± 2.160(0.0523) = 0.2613 ± 0.1130.

± 0.0292 divides SEb by √n again: the standard error already allows for the sample size. ± 0.1025 uses z* = 1.960, but σ is estimated, so t* is needed. ± 1.1681 uses S, the spread of the residuals, instead of the standard error of the slope.

energetics-1-01.solution:
Binding needs a compatible shape and charge. The lysine’s + charge attracted the substrate’s − charge; aspartate’s − charge repels it, so the enzyme–substrate complex forms less readily and the rate falls.

Charge matters as much as shape, so “unchanged” is wrong. An extra charge only helps if it is opposite to the substrate’s. Enzymes are not consumed; a charge change does not make the binding covalent.

atoms-1-01.solution:
Grams to moles with the molar mass, then moles to atoms with Avogadro’s number:

3.50 g55.85 g/mol=0.06267 mol;0.06267×6.022×1023=3.77×1022\frac{3.50\ \text{g}}{55.85\ \text{g/mol}} = 0.06267\ \text{mol};\quad 0.06267 \times 6.022\times10^{23} = 3.77\times10^{22}55.85 g/mol3.50 g​=0.06267 mol;0.06267×6.022×1023=3.77×1022

1.18 × 1026 multiplies by the molar mass instead of dividing. 2.11 × 1024 treats grams as moles. 9.61 × 1024 inverts the mass-to-mole step.

evolution-1-01.solution:
Variation in colour already existed and was heritable. Brown beetles left more offspring, so the brown phenotype, and its alleles, rose in frequency: natural selection.

Individuals do not change their inherited colour and pass it on; that is the inheritance of acquired traits. Predators select among existing variants; they do not cause mutations. Mutations are random with respect to need: a population cannot evolve a trait because it needs it.

slopes-2-05.solution:
R-Sq = r2 = 0.827, so r = ±√0.827 = ±0.909. The slope is negative, so r = −0.909.

0.909 has the wrong sign. −0.827 forgets the square root. −0.416 takes the root of 1 − R-Sq, the share of variation the line leaves unexplained.

cells-1-01.solution:
Each location’s label peaks in turn: the rough ER at 3 min, the Golgi at 20 min, secretory vesicles at 60 min, and outside the cell at 120 min. So the protein is made on ribosomes bound to the rough ER, modified and packaged in the Golgi, carried in vesicles, and released by exocytosis.

Putting the Golgi first ignores that the ER is labelled earliest. Placing vesicles before the Golgi contradicts the Golgi’s peak at 20 min, before the vesicles’ at 60 min. Starting in the vesicles reverses the whole path.

thermochem-1-01.solution:
The water is the surroundings, and its temperature fell, so it lost energy. That energy went into the system (the dissolving solid), which absorbed it: the process is endothermic, ΔH > 0.

A falling temperature means the surroundings lost heat, not that the system did; an exothermic process warms the water. Energy cannot flow from the solid to the water if the water is cooling. Breaking a solid apart costs energy; it never releases it.

substances-1-01.solution:
All four are nonpolar: two identical atoms share the electrons equally. The only intermolecular force is London dispersion, which grows with the number of electrons, from 18 to 106: a bigger, more polarizable cloud forms larger temporary dipoles.

The molecules are not polar at all, so there are no dipole–dipole forces. Boiling separates molecules; it does not break the X–X bonds (and the I–I bond is in fact the weakest of them). There is no hydrogen in these molecules, so no hydrogen bonding.

kinetics-1-01.solution:
The coefficients fix the ratio: 6 H2 form for every 4 PH3 used, so H2 forms 6/4 as fast: 4.8 × 10−4 × 6/4 = 7.2 × 10−4 M/s.

3.2 × 10−4 M/s inverts the ratio. 4.8 × 10−4 M/s ignores the coefficients. 1.2 × 10−4 M/s is the rate of reaction (or of P4 formation), not of H2.

contact-2-08.solution:
152,373 ÷ 50,762 ≈ 3.0. The trade grew with the sugar plantations of Brazil and the Caribbean.

0.33 divides the wrong way. 2.5 compares with 1551–1575, and 11.4 with 1501–1525, not the period asked about.

reactions-1-01.solution:
The metal is used up and a gas with a new property (it burns with a pop: hydrogen) appears, so new substances formed. This is Mg + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2.

Water boiling at 100 °C makes bubbles of water vapour: same substance, physical change. The violet vapour is iodine subliming and depositing again: a colour change, but the same substance. The white solid dissolved and was recovered unchanged by evaporation: physical.

colonial-3-01.solution:
From 1700 to 1740 the southern share rose from 21.5% to 31.6%, while New England’s moved from 1.8% to 2.9% and the middle colonies’ stayed between about 7 and 11%. As plantation slavery took hold, the South imported many more enslaved Africans.

Slavery was legal in every British colony, including New England and the middle colonies, which held significant minorities of enslaved people in their port cities. The southern share was the highest in every year shown, and it rose.

equilibrium-1-01.solution:
Equilibrium is dynamic: both reactions keep going, at the same rate, so no amount changes and the colour holds steady.

The reactions do not stop; only the net change does. Equal rates do not mean equal concentrations: their ratio is set by K. And N2O4 is still present at equilibrium; if it were gone the reverse reaction would make more.

colonial-1-01.solution:
New France’s wealth was fur, which only Native hunters could supply, so French traders lived among Native peoples, married into their families and joined their alliances; few French farmers came. English colonists came in large numbers, in families and as servants, to farm, and lived apart from Native peoples.

The encomienda was Spanish, not French. The plantation-versus-fur-trade choice reverses the two empires, and so does the family-farming choice.

revolution-1-02.solution:
Franklin’s plan for a common council was rejected by every colonial assembly (and by Britain): each colony guarded its own powers. “Join, or Die” was a call the colonies did not answer in 1754.

Independence was not on the table in 1754; the plan kept the Crown at its head. It was a colonial plan, not a parliamentary tax scheme, and Native nations did not demand it.

revolution-5-02.solution:
From 1793 France and Britain were at war; Federalists leaned to Britain, Republicans to France; the Neutrality Proclamation, the Genêt affair and Jay’s Treaty all turned on it. Washington urged neutrality and national unity, warning too against parties.

Florida was not purchased until 1819; the British burned Washington in 1814; and there was no alliance with Britain against the Barbary States.

republic-1-01.solution:
Marbury struck down part of the Judiciary Act of 1789 as unconstitutional, establishing judicial review: the Court, not Congress or the states, decides finally what the Constitution means.

The Bank was upheld in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819); “domestic dependent nations” is Cherokee Nation v. Georgia (1831); the commerce power was the issue in Gibbons v. Ogden (1824).

revolution-3-04.solution:
Congress could not tax; giving it a revenue required amending the Articles, which needed every state. One small state could block it.

Congress could declare war and make treaties; each state had one vote regardless of population; and there were no national courts under the Articles.

contact-2-01.solution:
From 25.2 million in 1518 to 1.075 million in 1605 is a fall of about 96%. Epidemics of Old World diseases, war, forced labor and famine caused it. Other historians estimate a much smaller starting population, but every estimate shows a catastrophe.

The numbers keep falling through 1605: no recovery. The drop is steepest early and slows later, not equal each year. The first figure is from 1518, the eve of the conquest; the table says nothing about decline before contact.

electrochem-1-01.solution:
A solid gives a gas: 0 mol of gas become 1 mol, and gas particles are far more dispersed than those of a solid, so the entropy rises.

Condensing a gas to a liquid confines the particles: ΔS < 0. 2SO2 + O2 → 2SO3 turns 3 mol of gas into 2, and N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3 turns 4 into 2: fewer gas particles, fewer arrangements, ΔS < 0.

acids-1-01.solution:
pH = −log(2.5 × 10−4) = 3.60, and at 25 °C pH + pOH = 14.00, so pOH = 14.00 − 3.60 = 10.40.

3.60 is the pH, not the pOH. 9.60 comes from adding log 2.5 to 4 instead of subtracting it, which gives pH 4.40. 10.0 uses only the power of ten and ignores the 2.5.

worldwars-1-03.solution:
Two thirds of the 84 senators voting is 56; the treaty got 57, one more. The narrow margin shows how divided the country was over taking the Philippines.

A treaty needs two thirds, not a majority. Hawaii, not the Philippines, was annexed by joint resolution (1898). 27 senators voted no.

coldwar-1-01.solution:
Britain told the US in February 1947 that it could no longer aid Greece and Turkey; Truman asked Congress for $400 million to keep them out of the Soviet orbit. This was the first statement of containment as a global policy.

The Berlin blockade began in June 1948, the Korean War in June 1950 and Sputnik in October 1957, all after the speech.

present-2-04.solution:
Seats are reapportioned after each census by population. Texas gained 11 and Florida 9 while New York lost 8 and Ohio 6: the Sun Belt grew faster than the Rust Belt and Northeast, gaining political weight.

The House has had 435 seats since 1913; seats moved, they were not added. The US population grew. The Great Migration of African Americans to the North was a pattern of the early and mid-twentieth century, and the table shows the reverse direction.

gilded-1-01.solution:
The Pacific Railway Act (1862) and later acts gave the Union Pacific, Central Pacific and other lines alternate sections of public land along their routes and federal loans by the mile: subsidies that made private construction profitable.

The government did not build or run the lines; private companies did. Federal limits on state rate-setting came only with Wabash (1886). Railroads hired Irish immigrants, veterans and, on the Central Pacific, thousands of Chinese laborers.

republic-3-04.solution:
Turnout rose from 26.9% in 1824 to 80.2% in 1840 as states replaced property qualifications with white manhood suffrage, chose electors by popular vote, and as Democrats and Whigs built mass parties and campaigns.

The Fifteenth Amendment came in 1870. Women could not vote in any state then (New Jersey ended it in 1807). Primaries are a twentieth-century reform.

coldwar-3-01.solution:
Plessy had upheld “separate but equal” railroad cars in 1896, the legal foundation of Jim Crow. Brown, argued by Thurgood Marshall for the NAACP and decided 9–0, rejected it for public schools.

Dred Scott denied Black citizenship and was undone by the Fourteenth Amendment; Marbury established judicial review; Korematsu upheld wartime incarceration of Japanese Americans.

civilwar-4-01.solution:
Winfield Scott’s plan would squeeze the Confederacy: cut its trade with a blockade and take the Mississippi, dividing it in two. The blockade began in April 1861; Vicksburg completed the river in July 1863.

“On to Richmond” was the popular demand Scott’s plan resisted. The plan was military, not a peace proposal, and Britain stayed neutral.

gilded-3-04.solution:
The Knights (1869; under Powderly about 700,000 members by 1886) welcomed nearly all workers except the Chinese and sought a “cooperative commonwealth.” The AFL (1886) organized skilled crafts for “pure and simple” goals: wages, hours, contracts.

The second choice describes the AFL; the Knights came first; they admitted many immigrants (excluding Chinese).

present-1-01.solution:
Reagan’s answer to “government is the problem” was to shrink its claims on the economy: supply-side tax cuts (the top rate fell from 70% to 50%) and continued deregulation.

Medicare and Medicaid and federal school aid are Great Society programs of 1965 that expanded government; the EPA (1970) expanded federal regulation. These are the liberal policies the New Right criticized.

worldwars-4-01.solution:
Italy’s quota fell by 91%, and Italy, Poland, Russia and Greece together fell from 100,902 to 12,175 (88%); Germany fell by only 24%. Basing quotas on the 1890 census, before most southern and eastern Europeans arrived, was the point.

No quota rose; the cuts were deliberately unequal; Germany lost a smaller share than Italy.

gilded-5-02.solution:
The Gospel of Wealth: the rich are trustees for the public and should give, wisely, while alive. Carnegie funded libraries, concert halls and universities.

He opposed government redistribution; he defended wealth, not condemned it; worker ownership was a socialist or Knights of Labor idea.

gilded-2-03.solution:
Louisiana’s 1898 constitution imposed a poll tax, a literacy (or property) test and a grandfather clause that exempted only men whose fathers or grandfathers could vote before 1867, that is, whites. Registration fell by more than 99 percent.

The Exodusters’ migration (1879) was far too small and too early; the Nineteenth Amendment (1920) gave women the vote; Brown (1954) came half a century later.

republic-6-01.solution:
The import ban took effect in 1808, yet the enslaved population grew from 893,602 in 1800 to 3,204,313 in 1850: births exceeded deaths. The domestic trade moved people within the country but did not add to the total.

The legal Atlantic trade (including Charleston’s, reopened 1803–07) ended in 1808, and smuggling was small. Kidnapping of free people happened but was far too rare to explain the numbers; Caribbean imports were banned along with African ones.

civilwar-1-01.solution:
The writer claims a providential right (“allotted by Providence”) to spread across “the continent,” for Americans’ “free development”: the core of Manifest Destiny, used to justify annexing Texas.

The excerpt is continental, not overseas. It says nothing about slavery, and far from respecting rival claims it was written to defend annexation.

coldwar-4-01.solution:
US forces rose from about 16,300 advisers to about 184,300 troops. Congress passed the Tonkin Resolution in August 1964 (House 416–0, Senate 88–2); bombing and ground troops followed in March 1965.

Tet came in 1968, the Paris Accords in 1973 and the War Powers Resolution in 1973.

adas-3-02.solution:
Better-educated workers produce more: human capital raises the economy’s productive capacity, pushing the production possibilities curve out and LRAS right.

More consumer spending shifts AD, not LRAS. The price level is on the vertical axis: a change in it moves along curves, and LRAS doesn’t depend on it at all. A temporary fall in oil prices lowers costs in the short run: it shifts SRAS, not potential output.

money-2-02.solution:
The realized real rate is 8% − 6% = 2%, below the 5% both expected. The borrower repays dollars that buy less than expected: unexpected inflation moves purchasing power from lenders to borrowers.

5% is the real rate they expected, not the one that happened. A fixed nominal rate is exactly why someone gains: the rate could not adjust to the surprise. Adding inflation to the nominal rate has the sign wrong.

scarcity-1-01.solution:
Scarcity is the basic economic problem: unlimited wants, limited resources. It applies to every person and every economy, which is why every choice has an opportunity cost.

A good unavailable at the current price is a shortage, a market at a price below equilibrium; it can be ended by a price rise, and scarcity cannot. Rich countries face scarcity too, since their wants grow with their means. Rising prices in general are inflation, not scarcity.

indicators-1-02.solution:
GDP = C + I + G + (X − M) = 520 + 140 + 180 + (60 − 75) = $825 billion.

$915 adds transfer payments, which buy no output. $975 adds imports instead of subtracting them. $955 also counts the stock purchases, a financial transaction that produces nothing.

adas-2-02.solution:
Spending adds 50 × 10 = 500; the tax takes away 50 × 9 = 450. Net: +50, the change in G. The balanced-budget multiplier is 1, whatever the MPC.

‘No change’ forgets that the tax multiplier is smaller than the spending multiplier: part of the tax comes out of saving. 500 ignores the tax. 950 adds the tax’s effect instead of subtracting it.

scarcity-1-06.solution:
Moving from C to D, guns fall from 14 to 8: the 14 − 8 = 6 guns given up are the opportunity cost of the extra unit of butter.

4 guns is the cost of the previous unit (B to C). 8 is the number of guns still produced at D, and 14 the number at C: opportunity cost is the change, not a level.

adas-4-06.solution:
An inflationary gap calls for contractionary policy: less spending (lower G) and less disposable income (higher taxes). Both shift AD left, toward full-employment output.

Higher G with lower taxes is expansionary and widens the gap. Raising G and taxes equally is a balanced-budget change with a multiplier of 1: it shifts AD right. Lower taxes with higher transfers is expansionary.

scarcity-2-06.solution:
With output figures, the cost of one good is the other good divided by it: N gives up 30 rice for 10 tablets, so 1 tablet costs 30/10 = 3 tons of rice.

0.33 is N’s cost of 1 ton of rice, in tablets. 2 is Country S’s cost of a tablet. 30 is N’s total rice output, the cost of all 10 tablets rather than one.

money-1-01.solution:
Liquidity is how easily an asset can be used to pay, or turned into money, without losing value. A checking balance is money already: it can be spent directly.

A bond and a share must first be sold, and their prices may have moved. A house takes the longest to sell and may sell for less than hoped: the least liquid of the four.

adas-1-06.solution:
The spending multiplier is 1/(1 − MPC) = 1/(1 − 0.75) = 4. Any first change in spending, investment included, is multiplied: 40 × 4 = 160.

40 ignores the later rounds of spending. 30 is only the second round (MPC × 40). 53.3 divides by the MPC instead of by the MPS. It is the maximum because, with an upward-sloping SRAS, part of the shift in AD raises the price level instead of output.

money-1-04.solution:
A buyer can now earn 9% on new bonds, so will pay only what makes the old bond earn 9% too: $1,060 ÷ 1.09 = $972.48. The price falls below $1,000.

$1,000 ignores the rise in rates: no one pays that for a bond earning 6% when new ones earn 9%. $1,060.00 is what it pays in a year, not what that payment is worth today. Discounting only the face value forgets the $60 of interest.

adas-1-01.solution:
The interest-rate effect: at a higher price level people need more money for the same purchases, so money demand rises, interest rates rise, and interest-sensitive spending, chiefly investment, falls.

Lower purchasing power of savings reducing consumption is the real wealth effect. Domestic goods becoming dearer than foreign ones is the exchange-rate (foreign purchases) effect. Both are real reasons AD slopes down, but they are not the interest-rate effect. A central bank lowering rates is monetary policy, not part of the AD curve’s slope, and the direction is wrong: lower interest rates would raise spending as prices rise.

indicators-3-05.solution:
Inflation rate = (135 − 125) ÷ 125 × 100 = 8.0%.

10 is the change in index points, not a percentage of the starting level. 7.4% divides by the later year’s index. 35% is the rise since the base year, not over this one year.

indicators-2-04.solution:
The labor force is 150 + 10 = 160 million. Unemployment rate = unemployed ÷ labor force = 10 ÷ 160 = 6.25%.

4.00% divides by the whole adult population, including people not in the labor force. 6.67% divides by the employed only. 64.00% is the labor-force participation rate.

scarcity-4-04.solution:
At equilibrium Qd = Qs: 200 − 10P = 50 + 20P, so 150 = 30P and P = $5.00, with Q = 150.

$20.00 is the price at which quantity demanded falls to zero, not where the curves meet. $6.67 ignores the supply intercept of 50. $8.33 adds the intercepts instead of subtracting them.

stabilization-1-01.solution:
Paying for the bonds adds to banks’ reserves; banks lend more and the money supply rises. In the money market the nominal interest rate falls, interest-sensitive spending (investment) rises, and AD shifts right.

The second chain is a bond sale. The third has the rate moving the wrong way, and monetary policy shifts AD, not aggregate supply, in the short run. The fourth ends with AD falling, which more investment spending cannot cause.

stabilization-4-03.solution:
Government borrowing adds to the demand for loanable funds (or, read as negative public saving, reduces their supply). Either way the real interest rate rises, and private borrowers, facing the higher rate, invest less: crowding out.

Private investment demand slopes downward, so a higher rate cannot raise it. A lower real rate would need more saving or less borrowing.

trade-1-02.solution:
A gift sent abroad is a unilateral transfer, part of the current account, and money leaves the United States: a debit.

The Japanese tourist’s spending is a U.S. export of a service: money flows in, a current-account credit. The German purchase of shares is an asset transaction, recorded in the capital and financial account (a credit there), not the current account. Dividends received from abroad are income from abroad flowing in: a current-account credit.

stabilization-2-01.solution:
Higher AD raises real output (so unemployment falls) and the price level (so inflation rises): a move up and to the left along the existing SRPC.

A shift of the SRPC comes from a change in expected inflation or an aggregate supply shock, not from AD. Down and to the right is what a decrease in AD does. The LRPC moves only when the natural rate of unemployment changes.

foundations-1-01.solution:
Government’s ‘just powers’ come from ‘the consent of the governed’: authority rests with the people, which is popular sovereignty.

Federalism is the division of power between national and state governments, which the Declaration does not set up. Separation of powers divides power among branches, a design of the Constitution. Judicial review is the courts’ power to strike down laws, established in 1803 and not mentioned here.

stabilization-5-01.solution:
More human capital raises productivity: the economy can produce more at full employment, so LRAS (and the PPC) shifts out.

Transfers and consumer optimism raise aggregate demand, not capacity. A lower price level is a movement along the curves, not a shift of LRAS.

stabilization-2-06.solution:
As people come to expect the higher inflation, the SRPC shifts up and wages catch up: unemployment drifts back to the natural rate, now with higher inflation. The LRPC is vertical: there is no lasting trade-off.

Holding unemployment below the natural rate would need ever-faster inflation, not stable inflation. Inflation does not return to its old rate while money keeps growing. Unemployment above the natural rate with falling inflation describes a disinflation, the opposite policy.

stabilization-3-01.solution:
From MV = PQ, velocity is nominal GDP ÷ money: 1800/450 = 4. Each dollar is spent 4 times a year on final goods and services.

0.25 divides the wrong way. 1350 subtracts instead of dividing. 2 halves the right answer.

stabilization-5-04.solution:
Years to double ≈ 70 ÷ growth rate = 70/2.5 = 28 years.

17.5 multiplies instead of dividing; 40 uses 100 instead of 70, which ignores compounding; 14 is half the doubling time.

money-5-04.solution:
With ample reserves the demand for reserves is flat at the interest on reserve balances (IORB) rate, and the supply of reserves sits on that flat part. The Fed moves the federal funds rate by moving its administered rates: lowering IORB (and the overnight reverse repo rate) lowers the funds rate.

Selling bonds would shift supply left along the flat part and barely move the rate (and in the wrong direction for this goal). Raising the reserve requirement or IORB is contractionary.

money-2-05.solution:
M1 = currency + demand deposits + other liquid deposits = 300 + 500 + 900 = $1,700 billion. M2 = M1 + small time deposits + retail money market funds = $1,700 + 200 + 400 = $2,300 billion.

$1,700 billion is M1 only. $1,900 billion leaves out money market funds. Credit card balances are not money at all: they are loans, repaid with money. (Since May 2020 savings deposits count in M1; under older definitions they were in M2 only. M2 is $2,300 billion either way.)

trade-5-02.solution:
A foreigner buying a U.S. asset sends money into the United States in exchange for an asset: a financial capital inflow, a credit in the U.S. capital and financial account.

A U.S. firm building a factory abroad is foreign direct investment going out: an outflow. Buying a foreign car is an import, a current-account debit. Interest paid to foreigners is income flowing out, a current-account debit.

trade-2-05.solution:
To buy U.S. goods, services or assets, foreigners must first buy dollars: that is the demand for dollars.

U.S. residents buying foreign things sell dollars for foreign currency: they create the supply of dollars. The dollar floats, so the Fed does not buy dollars to fix its value. Banks’ reserves are a domestic matter, not a source of demand in the foreign exchange market (and U.S. reserve requirements have been zero since March 2020).

stabilization-4-01.solution:
The debt is a stock: it rises by each deficit and falls by each surplus. 4 + 0.3 + 0.25 − 0.1 + 0.2 = $4.65 trillion.

$4.85 trillion adds the surplus as if it were a deficit. $0.65 trillion is only the change in the debt. $4.1 trillion counts only the surplus, and the wrong way.

money-4-05.solution:
Expansionary policy: buying bonds adds reserves, the money supply rises, the interest rate falls, interest-sensitive spending (investment, and consumption of durables) rises, and AD shifts right, raising real GDP and employment.

Selling bonds drains reserves and raises rates. Buying bonds lowers rates, it does not raise them. And monetary policy works on aggregate demand, not aggregate supply.

branches-1-05.solution:
Cloture on legislation needs three-fifths of the senators duly chosen and sworn: 3/5 × 95 = 57.0, so 57.

60 is three-fifths of a full Senate of 100. 48 is a majority, which since 2013 and 2017 ends debate on nominations, not bills. 64 is two-thirds, the threshold for treaties and overrides.

branches-5-04.solution:
Congress fixes the size of the Supreme Court by statute (nine since 1869), creates the lower courts, and can regulate appellate jurisdiction.

Executive orders are the president’s. Declaring rulings unconstitutional is not a congressional power. Certiorari is granted by the justices.

branches-3-01.solution:
Under Article I, Section 7, a bill not returned within ten days becomes law unless Congress, by its adjournment, prevents its return; then it is a pocket veto. There is nothing to override.

A bill becomes law without a signature only if Congress is in session at the end of the ten days. An override needs a returned (regular) veto. Courts do not review bills before they are law.

foundations-2-04.solution:
Congress could requisition money from the states but not tax; states often did not pay, leaving the government unable to pay its debts or support an army.

There was no president or national executive under the Articles. There were no national courts. Each state had one vote, regardless of size.

foundations-5-03.solution:
The commerce power reaches economic activity that substantially affects interstate commerce; possessing a gun in a school zone is neither, and is left to the states’ police powers.

The decision rested on the commerce clause, not the Second Amendment. It left states free to regulate guns near schools (Texas already did). Congressional findings were discussed, but their absence was not the ground of decision.

branches-2-03.solution:
Cracking spreads A’s 210 voters at 42% in every district: A loses all 5. Packing B: A needs 51 of 100 to win a district, so A can win ⌊210/51⌋ = 4, with B packed into the rest.

2 and 2 is roughly proportional representation, which neither mapmaker would draw. 0 and 2 understates what packing can do. A cannot win 5: that would take 255 voters.

foundations-5-01.solution:
Chief Justice Marshall, for a unanimous Court: the bank was a legitimate means to enumerated ends (an implied power under the necessary and proper clause), and by the supremacy clause a state may not tax an instrument of the national government, since ‘the power to tax involves the power to destroy’.

Banking need not be enumerated: that was Maryland’s losing argument. Taxing is concurrent, but not a state tax on a federal institution. Judicial review of acts of Congress was Marbury v. Madison (1803).

foundations-2-01.solution:
Madison accepts that factions cannot be removed without destroying liberty, so he controls their effects: in a large republic, many factions check one another and no single one easily forms a majority.

Giving everyone the same opinions is the remedy Madison rejects as impracticable. A small, homogeneous republic is Brutus’s position, not Madison’s. Relying on the states is the Anti-Federalist view.

branches-6-03.solution:
Hearings and investigations are oversight; using appropriations to reward or punish an agency is the power of the purse.

The president appoints and removes, not the committee. No court is involved. Notice and comment is how the agency itself makes rules.

foundations-3-03.solution:
Madison wanted each branch to have the means and motive to resist the others: the veto and override set the president’s ambition against Congress’s, a check and balance.

Ratification by nine states is how the Constitution came into force, not a check between branches. Reserved powers are federalism (the Tenth Amendment). Apportionment by population concerns representation.

branches-4-01.solution:
Appealing directly to the public so that it pressures Congress is going public, from the bully pulpit of the presidency.

No order directing the executive branch is issued. A pocket veto kills a bill after adjournment. Senatorial courtesy concerns nominations in a senator’s home state.

foundations-1-07.solution:
Organized groups compete, and policy emerges from their contest: the pluralist model.

Participatory democracy stresses broad individual participation, not group bargaining. Elite democracy gives influence to a small wealthy or educated few rather than to many competing groups. No referendum took place.

branches-1-01.solution:
Advice and consent on appointments belongs to the Senate alone; it confirms judges and executive officers by majority vote.

Revenue bills must originate in the House (Article I, Section 7). Impeachment (bringing charges) is the House’s power; the Senate tries the case. Overriding a veto needs two-thirds of both chambers, so it is not the Senate’s alone.

branches-4-05.solution:
Under the rule of four, four justices’ votes grant certiorari; the Court grants few of the petitions it receives.

A majority decides the case, not whether to hear it. Most review is discretionary, not mandatory. The solicitor general argues for the government and files briefs but does not set the Court’s docket.

foundations-4-02.solution:
Licensing professions is part of the states’ police powers over health and safety: a reserved power.

Tariffs on imports are national (regulating foreign commerce; states may not tax imports without Congress’s consent). Admitting states and establishing post offices are powers delegated to Congress.

ideologies-2-07.solution:
In a random sample every member of the population has an equal chance of being chosen; drawing by chance from a complete list does that, and gives a representative sample.

Capitol visitors and website readers choose themselves and are not typical of all adults. Fixed numbers from the largest cities leave out everyone else in the state, so they have no chance of being chosen.

liberties-1-01.solution:
The First Amendment begins “Congress shall make no law,” and in Barron v. Baltimore (1833) the Court held the Bill of Rights restrained only the national government. After the Fourteenth Amendment (1868), the Court applied most of its protections to the states one at a time (selective incorporation).

It did not bind the states in 1791; that is exactly what Barron rejected. It was aimed at the new national government, not the states. Only some amendments (IV–VIII) concern criminal procedure, and none is limited to federal trials by its terms.

branches-6-06.solution:
Two-year terms keep every House member close to the next election; only a third of the Senate faces voters at once, and each senator only every six years.

The Senate alone gives consent to treaties. Representatives have always been popularly elected (state legislatures chose senators before 1913). The Senate passes bills on its own; the president acts afterward.

ideologies-4-06.solution:
Supply-side fiscal policy lowers tax rates (and regulations) to increase incentives to produce: more work, saving and investment, and so more capacity to grow.

Spending on infrastructure and payments to households are Keynesian: they boost demand. Lowering interest rates is monetary policy, made by the Fed, not fiscal policy.

participation-1-01.solution:
The text binds “the United States” and “any State”, so it covers all elections, and it forbids denial “on account of age” to anyone 18 or older.

It is not limited to federal elections: “any State” reaches state elections too. It says nothing about registration, which states still run. It contains no military condition, though the draft of 18-year-olds during Vietnam was a leading argument for it.

participation-3-02.solution:
This is Duverger’s law: winner-take-all districts punish small parties, so votes for them are seen as wasted.

The Constitution does not mention parties at all. The House does not use proportional representation. Third parties may raise money under the same rules as any party.

liberties-1-06.solution:
The Court held that students do not “shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate.” Silent black armbands protesting the Vietnam War were protected because they caused no substantial disruption.

Offense alone is not enough. The armbands were symbolic speech, and protected. Schools may still restrict speech that substantially disrupts, or that is lewd or promotes illegal drug use (later cases), so the protection is not total.

liberties-4-03.solution:
A unanimous Court held that “separate educational facilities are inherently unequal,” rejecting Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) for public schools.

Upholding equal-but-separate schools was Plessy’s doctrine. The Civil Rights Act came ten years after Brown. The Court did not set a one-year deadline: Brown II (1955) ordered desegregation “with all deliberate speed.”

liberties-2-04.solution:
In a 6–3 per curiam opinion, the Court held that “any system of prior restraints of expression comes to this Court bearing a heavy presumption against its constitutional validity,” and the Nixon administration had not met its heavy burden. The Times and the Washington Post resumed publishing.

Classification alone did not justify a restraint. The Court did not withdraw First Amendment protection. Actual malice comes from New York Times v. Sullivan (1964), and it makes libel suits by officials harder, not easier.

liberties-3-03.solution:
Beginning with Gitlow v. New York (1925), the Court has held one right at a time to be fundamental and so binding on the states through the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause.

It is the Court’s doing, not Congress’s or the states’. The Fourteenth Amendment was ratified in 1868, but incorporation came gradually, over a century and more; it was never total.

participation-1-05.solution:
Choosing on expectations of future performance is prospective voting.

Retrospective voting judges a past record. Straight-ticket voting would follow her party whatever the plans. Political socialization is how people acquire political beliefs, not a model of a vote choice.

ideologies-2-03.solution:
Trust rose from 44% to 55%, an unusual increase. After the September 11 attacks Americans rallied around their government; Gallup found 60% trust in October 2001.

Watergate (1972–1974) came long before and lowered trust (36% in 1974). The financial crisis came in 2008, when trust fell to 31%. A shutdown or anger at Congress would push trust down, not up.

ideologies-3-06.solution:
The halves were chosen at random, so they are alike; the only difference was a word. A gap of 44.0 points from one changed word is a wording effect. The General Social Survey has found a gap of this kind for decades.

Random assignment makes the halves comparable, so who they were cannot explain the gap. A margin of error of a few points cannot explain 44.0. Both halves heard the same question apart from the term, so a general misunderstanding would affect both alike.

ideologies-1-02.solution:
Rule of law means that every person, even those in power, must follow and is accountable to the same laws. A president obeying a court order, as in United States v. Nixon (1974), is the clearest case.

Lowering taxes to encourage competition reflects free enterprise. Choosing one’s own path reflects individualism. Scholarships that widen access reflect equality of opportunity.

participation-2-01.solution:
75.2 − 47.7 = 27.5 percentage points.

57.7 is the gap as a percent of the young group’s rate, a relative difference. 61.5 is the average of the two rates. 52.3 is the share of 18- to 24-year-olds who did not vote.

participation-4-02.solution:
Issue networks are broad, shifting webs of experts and advocates who often disagree; iron triangles are closed and stable.

The committee–agency–group trio is the iron triangle itself. Networks span branches and outside experts, not only courts. They are informal, not agencies.

participation-4-05.solution:
Each state has as many electors as members of Congress: 14 representatives + 2 senators = 16.

14 leaves out the two senators. 15 adds one senator. 28 doubles the House seats, which has no basis in the Constitution.

participation-6-04.solution:
Programming aimed at an audience of one ideology, with a consistent slant, is ideologically oriented.

The free-rider problem concerns interest groups. A neutral gatekeeper would not consistently favor one side. Horse-race journalism is about who is ahead, not partisan commentary.

participation-5-03.solution:
The Court (5–4) struck down the ban on corporate and union independent expenditures and electioneering communications as a violation of free speech.

Direct corporate contributions to candidates remain banned. The Court upheld the disclaimer and disclosure rules, 8–1. The 60-day ban on corporate electioneering communications is exactly what it struck down.

kinematics-1-04.solution:
Distance adds up path, whichever way it goes. Watch it on the ball: up and back, every metre counts.

Displacement is only start to finish. The ball’s black arrow shrinks back to nothing when it returns, and so does the runner’s after a full lap.

So the lap is 400 m of distance and zero displacement: a path that comes back makes them differ.

So the lap is 400 m of distance and zero displacement: a path that comes back makes them differ.

kinematics-1-05.solution:
Displacement depends only on where the cart starts and ends, not on the turnaround in between:

Δx=xf−xi=−2.00−3.00=−5.00 m\Delta x = x_\text{f} - x_\text{i} = -2.00 - 3.00 = -5.00\ \text{m}Δx=xf​−xi​=−2.00−3.00=−5.00 m

5.00 m subtracts in the wrong order (xi − xf); 11.0 m is the distance travelled, and −2.00 m is the final position, not the change in position.

slips: That is the average velocity (displacement / time). Speed uses the whole path, including the bit back down.
That counts only the climb; by 1.70 s the ball is coming back down.

kinematics-1-07.solution:
0.50 s in: v = 9.80 − 9.80(0.50) = +4.90 m/s, the arrow pointing up.

0.50 s before landing: the arrow is just as long but points down, −4.90 m/s.

The flight is symmetric about the top, so matching moments have the same speed. Velocity carries direction, so the two are not identical.

0.50 s before landing: the arrow is just as long but points down, −4.90 m/s.
The flight is symmetric about the top, so matching moments have the same speed. Velocity carries direction, so the two are not identical.

kinematics-1-08.solution:
Average speed is total distance over total time. With each half of length d, the car spends longer on the slow half, so the slower speed counts more:

vavg=2dd/20.0+d/30.0=2(20.0)(30.0)20.0+30.0=24.0 m/sv_\text{avg} = \frac{2d}{d/20.0 + d/30.0} = \frac{2(20.0)(30.0)}{20.0 + 30.0} = 24.0\ \text{m/s}vavg​=d/20.0+d/30.02d​=20.0+30.02(20.0)(30.0)​=24.0 m/s

25.0 m/s averages the two speeds, which would only be right for equal times; 12.0 m/s drops the 2 in the total distance 2d.

limits-1-02.solution:
The instantaneous rate is the limit of the average rates as the interval shrinks to nothing:

lim⁡h→0(3+3h+h2)=3\lim_{h\to 0} (3 + 3h + h^2) = 3h→0lim​(3+3h+h2)=3

7 is the average rate over [1, 2] (h = 1); 1 is the value f(1), not a rate. Substituting h = 0 into the original quotient does give 0/0, but the limit is taken as h → 0, never at h = 0, and it exists.

limits-1-03.solution:
For x ≠ 4, (x−4)(x+4)x−4=x+4\frac{(x - 4)(x + 4)}{x - 4} = x + 4x−4(x−4)(x+4)​=x+4, which approaches 8. The limit only uses x ≠ 4, and f(4) = 3 is given separately.

The limit is not 3: the value at 4 has no effect on it. A limit and a value that disagree make f discontinuous, but the limit still exists. And f(4) is defined here: it is 3.

limits-1-04.solution:
The limit describes the outputs for inputs near 4, not at 4: they can be kept within any distance of 7 by keeping x close enough to 4.

g(4) may be 7, something else, or not defined; the limit doesn’t say. The second choice swaps the roles of input and output. And the values may approach 7 from above, below or both, so g(x) < 7 is not implied.

limits-1-05.solution:
From the left, x < 2, so only the first formula applies: lim⁡x→2−(x2−1)=3\lim_{x\to 2^-} (x^2 - 1) = 3limx→2−​(x2−1)=3.

−1 is the right-hand limit (and g(2)), from the other formula. The two-sided limit does not exist, since the sides disagree, but this one-sided limit does. 1 averages the two sides, which no limit does.

limits-1-06.solution:
The limit is the height the curve approaches, the open circle: 5. The value h(3) is the filled circle: 1. So the sum is 5 + 1 = 6.

10 reads the open circle as the value too; 2 reads the filled circle as the limit. The limit exists, since both sides approach 5; it just differs from h(3).

onevar-1-01.solution:
A statistical question expects variability in its answer: students differ in how much they sleep, so the answer is a distribution.

Maya’s sleep last night is one value for one person. The enrolment this year is a single count. The hours between 10 p.m. and 7 a.m. are fixed by the clock: no variation at all.

onevar-1-02.solution:
Individuals are the objects described by the data: one row each. Here every row is a dog seen that week.

Breeds are the values of one variable. The characteristics recorded are the variables (the columns), not the individuals. The veterinarian collects the data; she is not described by it.

onevar-1-03.solution:
A zip code is a number used as a label: it places a home in a group, and arithmetic on it means nothing (an average zip code is not a place). So it is categorical.

The number of siblings is a count, quantitative and discrete. Height and running time are measurements, quantitative and continuous.

onevar-1-04.solution:
A count of messages takes separate values (0, 1, 2, …) that can be listed: discrete.

Time and mass are measured on a continuous scale: any value in an interval is possible. A favourite app is a category, not a number.

onevar-1-06.solution:
The relative frequencies add to 1, so “no pet” is 1 − (0.45 + 0.30 + 0.10) = 0.15, and 0.15 × 80 = 12 households.

15 is the percent, not the count. 8 is the number with fish. 20 splits the households equally among the four categories.

problems.prompt: Which of the following is a statistical question?
choices: How many hours of sleep do students at this school get on a school night?
How many hours did Maya sleep last night?
How many students are enrolled at this school this year?
How many hours are there between 10 p.m. and 7 a.m.?

problems.prompt: A veterinarian records, for every dog seen at a clinic in one week, its breed, weight (kg), age (years), vaccinated (yes or no). What are the individuals in this data set?
choices: The breeds of the dogs
The dogs seen at the clinic that week
The 4 characteristics recorded
The veterinarian and the clinic

problems.prompt: Which of the following variables is categorical?

The zip code of a student’s home

problems.prompt: Which of the following is a discrete quantitative variable?

A person’s favourite app
The mass of a person’s phone, in grams
The number of text messages a person sends in a day
